questions.q: Under what conditions do real gases deviate most significantly from ideal behavior?
questions.explain: At low temperatures (slow moving particles) and high pressures (particles crowded together), intermolecular forces and particle volume become significant, causing deviation from the ideal model.

questions.q: In the Van der Waals equation $\left(P + \frac{n^2a}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT$, what does the constant '$b​$' correct for?
options: The finite volume occupied by the gas particles themselves.
questions.explain: The '$b​$' constant in the Van der Waals equation represents the excluded volume, correcting for the fact that real gas particles have a finite size and take up space.

questions.q: What is the primary reason real gases exert less pressure than ideal gases under certain conditions?
options: Intermolecular attractive forces pull particles together, reducing the force of impact on walls.
Real gas particles are softer and bounce less.
Real gas particles move slower at all temperatures.
Real gases chemically react with the container.
questions.explain: Intermolecular attractive forces (Van der Waals forces) pull gas particles toward one another. This retards their motion just before hitting the wall, reducing the impact force and thus the measured pressure.

questions.q: Which gas would you expect to behave most ideally at room temperature?
questions.explain: Helium is a small, monoatomic noble gas with extremely weak intermolecular forces (London dispersion only). Therefore, it follows the assumptions of the kinetic molecular theory (ideal gas) more closely than polar or larger molecules.
